question: Which statement best describes Implicit state sharing?
options: Before Context was ergonomic, parents injected state by iterating direct children with React.Children.map and cloning each with extra props via React.cloneElement. The fatal limitation is that it only reaches immediate children — wrap a Tab in a tooltip or div and the props land on the wrapper, silently disabling the inner component. It also can overwrite props the consumer set, so it's discouraged for anything but tiny, flat, fully-controlled sets.

Context is the modern, robust mechanism for compound components: the parent renders a Context.Provider with the shared state, and any descendant reads it with useContext regardless of nesting depth. Unlike cloneElement, it works through wrappers, fragments, and arbitrary reordering. A good practice is to throw a descriptive error from the consumer when context is null, catching misuse like a Tab rendered outside Tabs.

The defining trait of compound components is that the parent holds shared state and exposes it to children implicitly, so consumers never thread props between them. This solves prop-drilling and lets the consumer write clean, declarative JSX like <Tabs><Tab/></Tabs> where coordination is hidden. The state lives in one place (the parent) while children just declare themselves and read what they need.

Because children are just JSX the consumer arranges, a Context-based compound component imposes no fixed structure: children can be nested, wrapped, reordered, or styled freely without the parent enumerating them. This inversion of control is exactly why headless libraries adopt the pattern — they own behavior while consumers own layout. Avoid relying on children order or type so wrappers and reordering never break consumers.

question: Which statement best describes React.Children & cloneElement (legacy)?
options: A reusable compound component should support both modes: uncontrolled (the component owns state internally, seeded with defaultValue) and controlled (the parent owns state via value/onChange props). Internally you normalize to a single source of truth so the rest of the logic doesn't care which mode is active. This flexibility is what lets the same Tabs work for simple drop-in use and for cases where a parent needs to drive the active tab.

Every consumer of a context re-renders when the context value changes, so a naively built compound component can re-render its whole subtree on each interaction. The fixes are to memoize the provided value and to split a frequently-changing state context from a stable dispatch/setter context. Then clicking a tab only re-renders the tabs and panels that depend on the active value, not the entire tree.

question: Which statement best describes Accessibility (ARIA roles)?
options: Compound components are typically exported as a namespace — Tabs.List, Tabs.Tab, Tabs.Panel — by attaching sub-components as static properties of the root. This signals they belong together, improves discoverability and autocomplete, and keeps the public API cohesive. Co-locating the Context, root, and children in one module keeps the implicit contract maintainable.
